title: The unbroken reading
hookLine: the whole Granth read aloud without a break, taking about forty-eight hours

cards: It's three in the morning in a gurdwara. The hall is almost empty, the lights low, the city asleep. But at the front, one person is sitting behind the Guru Granth Sahib, reading aloud, steadily, page after page.

A few people sit wrapped in shawls, listening. In an hour or two, someone else will slide in beside the reader, pick up the line mid-sentence, and carry on, without a single second of silence in between.
It started two days ago. It won't stop until the last page.

teach.b: It's an akhand path. Akhand means unbroken, undivided; path means reading, recitation. So it's the unbroken reading: the whole Guru Granth Sahib, all 1,430 angs, read aloud from beginning to end without any break.

No one person can do it alone, so a team of readers, called pathis, take turns in shifts. When one reader's time is up, the next sits beside them and takes over the words mid-flow, so the reading is never interrupted.

Families and gurdwaras hold an akhand path for the big moments: gurpurabs, as you heard yesterday, and Vaisakhi, but also a wedding, a new baby, a new house, a death in the family, or simply to give thanks.
It begins with Ardas and karah prashad.
It ends with the bhog, the completion: the last pages are read, then Anand Sahib, Ardas, a hukamnama and prashad, often followed by langar. Nobody is expected to listen to all forty-eight hours.
People drop in, sit for a while, leave, come back. Some stay up through the night to keep the readers company. What matters is that the word keeps sounding, through the day and the dark.
There's another way too: a sahaj path, a steady reading of the whole Granth at your own pace, over weeks or months. Families sometimes do this at home.
Both come from the same wish: to hear the whole of the Guru's word, from Japji at the start to the last page, in order, all the way through.

how: For gurpurabs, family occasions and times of grief or thanks, Sikhs hold an akhand path: a team of readers takes turns to read the whole Guru Granth Sahib aloud without a break, over about forty-eight hours, ending with the bhog.

games.q: you're a reader, and your shift is ending. the next reader arrives. how do you hand over?
o: finish the page, pause, then let them start.
they sit beside you and take over mid-line.
stop for a short Ardas between readers.
games.why: the next reader picks up the words mid-flow, so there's not a second of silence: that's what akhand, unbroken, means.

practice: Play a recording of Gurbani being read, a path, if you can, or just sit. Picture yourself at three in the morning in that nearly empty hall, wrapped in a shawl, listening to a voice that hasn't stopped for a day and a half.
You don't need to understand; just keep it company.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: unbroken. One reader hands the line to the next, and the word never stops. Until tomorrow.
